text: Fahim had been trying to get a job at a software firm in Gulshan for the past four months. He had sent his first application in July but received no reply for six weeks. Then in late August, he got a call for a preliminary phone interview while he was visiting his parents in Rajshahi. He took the call standing outside on the veranda because the inside of the house had poor network coverage. A week after the phone screen, he was asked to come in for a written test at the company's office in Gulshan-2 on a specific Wednesday. He had already returned to Dhaka by then and was staying at his friend Zubair's flat in Shyamoli. The written test took three hours, and Fahim thought he had performed poorly in the algorithm section. But twelve days later, he received an email asking him to come back for a panel interview. This time he wore the blazer his mother had packed for him when he left Rajshahi three months ago. The panel interview was held in a glass-walled conference room on the seventh floor overlooking the lake at Gulshan. One of the interviewers mentioned that Fahim's first application had actually been shortlisted in July but had been misplaced due to an internal system error. The offer letter arrived two weeks after the panel interview, on a Tuesday. Fahim called his mother in Rajshahi immediately and then walked down to a tea shop near Shyamoli to sit and absorb the news quietly.

text: Riya's cousin Priya was getting married in the last week of November. On the 14th of November, Riya took a bus from Sylhet to Dhaka to help with the wedding preparations. She had bought the silk fabric for Priya's saree two months earlier from a boutique in Sylhet's Zindabazar. When she arrived at her aunt's apartment in Mirpur that evening, she found the entire living room buried under fabric rolls and stacks of invitation cards. Three days before Riya's arrival, the caterer had cancelled, sending the whole family into a panic. Riya spent the next morning calling every contact she had, and by afternoon she had found a replacement caterer in Mohammadpur who agreed to take over on short notice. On the 18th, her uncle flew in from Riyadh, where he had been working for the past two and a half years, and the apartment suddenly felt much livelier. That night at dinner, he mentioned that he had already wired money for the wedding from Saudi Arabia five weeks ago but had kept it secret to surprise everyone. On the morning of the 20th, Riya and Priya went to a parlour in Dhanmondi to finalize the bridal makeup look. On the way back, they stopped at the New Market to pick up bangles that had been ordered three weeks prior. The wedding ceremony was to be held at a community hall in Uttara on the 22nd. The night before the wedding, while everyone was decorating the hall, Riya realized she had left her own outfit back at the apartment in Mirpur. She had to take a CNG at midnight to retrieve it and returned just before one in the morning, exhausted but ready.

text: Arif's grandfather passed away on a Monday morning at the family home in Barisal. Arif was in Chittagong at the time, finishing up a work project that had kept him there for the past three weeks. He booked the earliest available launch ticket and arrived in Barisal early the next morning. The funeral prayers were held at the local mosque, the same mosque where his grandfather had led Juma prayers every Friday for nearly thirty years. After the burial, relatives from Dhaka, Khulna, and even a few from abroad began arriving throughout the day. Arif's aunt from Toronto, who had not visited Bangladesh in six years, landed at Hazrat Shahjalal Airport that afternoon and managed to catch a connecting flight to Barisal. Two days after the burial, the family gathered in the main sitting room of the ancestral house to go through old documents. Among the papers, they found a land deed dated 1968 and a photograph of a young man nobody immediately recognized. An elderly neighbour who had known the family for fifty years came over and identified the person as a younger brother of Arif's grandfather who had moved to Karachi before the liberation war and never returned. That evening, Arif walked to the river bank alone and sat there until the call for Isha prayer.

text: The bookshop in Purana Paltan that Kamal's father had opened in 1987 was finally going to be closed. Kamal had known it was coming since last spring when the landlord raised the rent by nearly forty percent. He had spent three weeks in April trying to find a new location around the area, but everything was either too small or too expensive. On a rainy afternoon in August, Kamal sat behind the old wooden counter going through the remaining inventory. The last major sale had been during the Ekushey Book Fair in February, six months ago, when a publisher set up a temporary stall beside the shop and brought in a crowd. A young woman came in that afternoon and spent nearly an hour browsing before buying a copy of a novel by Humayun Ahmed. She told him her father used to bring her to this exact shop every year during her childhood when they lived in Paltan. By November, the shelves had thinned out considerably. Kamal donated a large portion of the older stock to a school library in Wari that had reached out after hearing about the closure. On the last day before closing, his father traveled down from Narayanganj, where he had retired two years ago, to collect a few personal items from the back room. He stood at the entrance for a long moment before stepping inside and did not say much to Kamal all afternoon.

text: Rubel had been driving the same route between Mymensingh and Dhaka for eleven years. On a foggy December morning, he was flagged down near Tongi by a young woman carrying a large backpack and a sleeping child. She asked to be dropped near Farmgate. Halfway through the journey, stuck in traffic near the airport road, she told him she had come all the way from Netrokona the previous night after receiving a call that her husband had been admitted to a hospital in Dhaka three days ago following a workplace accident in a factory in Narayanganj. She had not slept since leaving. Rubel did not charge her the full fare. When he dropped her at Farmgate, he gave her directions to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, where most accident cases from Narayanganj were usually taken. He arrived home in Mymensingh that night later than usual. His wife had kept dinner warm. Over food, he mentioned the woman to her. His wife, who had worked as a nurse at Mymensingh Medical eight years ago, told him that injuries from weaving factory accidents were often far more serious than they appeared in the first two days.

text: Tanha's mother had been insisting for three years that she learn how to cook shorshe ilish properly. On the Friday before Eid ul Adha, Tanha finally agreed to a cooking session at their family home in Khulna. She had arrived from Dhaka the previous Monday on a Sundarban Express ticket she had bought six weeks in advance because the train fills up quickly before long holidays. Her mother had bought fresh hilsa from the Rupsha fish market that same morning, two large fish that the vendor said had been caught the night before from the Padma river. Tanha spent most of Thursday helping her younger sister hem a shalwar kameez that had come back from the tailor with uneven stitching. On Friday morning, she stood in the kitchen beside her mother for three hours learning each step. Her father came in twice to supervise and was told by her mother to go back to the living room both times. That evening, the family sat down on the wide veranda that overlooked the backyard where a mango tree her grandfather had planted forty years ago still stood. Tanha's uncle, who lived two streets away, came over as he always did on Fridays and confirmed that the shorshe Ilish was, by his estimation, actually better than last week's batch.

text: Jonas had been teaching English at a private school in Sylhet for two years when his contract was renewed for another year in April. He used the school's spring break in May to travel to Sreemangal for a few days. He had heard about the tea gardens from a colleague who had grown up in Moulvibazar. He took a local bus from Sylhet town early on a Thursday morning and arrived before noon at a guesthouse about three kilometers from Lawachara National Park. That afternoon he walked through one of the tea estates and met an elderly worker who had been picking tea on those same hills for thirty-five years. On his second day he hired a local guide and entered the forest early in the morning. They spotted a pair of hoolock gibbons in the canopy about forty minutes into the walk. The guide mentioned that five years ago the gibbons were far more numerous but deforestation on the eastern edge had steadily reduced their territory. On Friday evening, Jonas sat in a small tea shop at the Sreemangal bazaar and wrote notes in his journal. He returned to Sylhet on Sunday morning and was back at school by Monday, where his students immediately asked whether he had brought them anything. He had bought two packets of locally blended tea from a shop near the bus stand, which he left in the teachers' lounge.

text: Shirin's research project on urban water quality had required her to collect samples from three different rivers over the course of six months. The project had started the previous January when her supervisor at the university in Dhaka approved a proposal she had submitted four months earlier in September. The first collection trip was to the Buriganga in late January. She had done a preliminary survey of that area two years ago as part of her undergraduate thesis, so the banks were familiar. The samples from that trip revealed heavy metal contamination levels she had not expected, which delayed her analysis timeline by three weeks while she recalibrated her equipment. In March, she traveled to Mymensingh to collect samples from the Brahmaputra. A local environmental NGO that operated an office near the river helped her access certain restricted areas. Back in Dhaka, her lab assistant accidentally mislabeled two of the sample bottles from that trip, and she had to return to Mymensingh the following month to collect replacement samples. The final collection trip in June was to the Meghna in Chandpur, which she reached by launch from Sadarghat. On the boat back she met a retired government engineer who had worked on a flood control project on the Meghna in the early nineties. He described changes in the river's course over thirty years that she found directly relevant to her analysis.

text: Biplob had not been back to his village in Faridpur since his mother's second marriage, which had taken place seven years ago at the neighbor's courtyard. He returned now because his grandmother was ill. His office in Dhaka's Motijheel district had granted him five days of emergency leave. The night bus from Gulistan dropped him at Faridpur town at three in the morning, and a younger cousin picked him up on a motorbike for the remaining twelve kilometers to the village. text: The old neighbourhood football tournament in Wari had been held every year during the winter months for as long as anyone could remember. This year, Imran's team made it to the final for the first time in four years. Imran had moved away from Wari to Mirpur eight months ago for his new job, but he returned every weekend to practice with the team on the narrow concrete pitch behind the community mosque. The final was scheduled for a Friday afternoon in mid-December on the ground near the old post office, the same ground where Imran's older brother had once scored a hat-trick in a final twelve years ago. On the Thursday evening before the match, Imran stayed at his parents' old flat in Wari, which was now occupied by his uncle's family. In the morning, he walked to the nearby bakery on Rankin Street that he and his teammates used to visit as kids. It had changed owners twice since then but still sold the same sesame-covered bread rolls. The match ended in a draw after extra time and went to penalties. Imran converted his spot kick. When the team won, his mother called from their new house in Demra, where his parents had moved three years ago, having heard the result from a neighbor who had been watching. She told him to come for dinner. He took the bus from Wari to Demra and arrived in time for Isha.

text: Muna had been studying architecture at a university in Chittagong and had taken a semester off the previous year to travel and document colonial-era buildings across Bangladesh. She had started in Dhaka, spending two weeks photographing structures in Purana Dhaka that dated from the Mughal period and later the British era. She stayed with a family friend in Narinda during that stretch. From Dhaka she took a train to Rajshahi in the third week of her trip, where the Varendra Research Museum and several structures near the Padma riverfront kept her busy for nearly a week. A professor she had met at a seminar in Chittagong six months before the trip had given her a list of lesser-known sites in Rajshahi district that she would have otherwise missed. In Rajshahi she also visited a crumbling zamindar estate in a village about twenty kilometers outside the city that had not been officially documented. On her way back to Chittagong at the end of the semester leave, she stopped in Comilla for two days to photograph the Shalban Vihara complex. The image she took of the main stupa at golden hour ended up being selected for a photography exhibition in Dhaka eight months later. She was in Chittagong attending a studio review when she received the email, and she had to ask her friend in Dhaka to represent her at the exhibition opening.

text: Tariq owned a small garments workshop in Narsingdi that he had started with his brother nine years ago. In the summer, their biggest buyer, a wholesaler based in Narayanganj who had been ordering from them since the workshop's second year, suddenly cancelled a large order two weeks before the delivery date. Tariq drove to Narayanganj the next morning to meet the wholesaler in person at his office near the river. The meeting lasted two hours and resolved nothing. On his way back, stuck in traffic near the Dhaka-Chittagong highway junction, Tariq called an old contact in Gazipur who sometimes sourced orders for smaller workshops. The contact mentioned a buyer in Old Dhaka who was looking for a new supplier after their previous one had shut down three months ago due to a factory fire. Tariq visited the Old Dhaka buyer the following Thursday and walked through the narrow lanes of Islampur to reach his shop. They agreed on a smaller initial order to test the quality. Six weeks later, that buyer became their second largest account. Tariq's brother, who had been running the production floor in Narsingdi throughout all of this, learned about the new deal when he called one evening and heard Tariq sounding cheerful for the first time in a month.

text: Jharna had been quilting for most of her life, a skill she had learned from her own mother in the village of Pabna where she was born. She now lived in a cramped but tidy flat in Demra, Dhaka, with her husband and two sons. Every December she made at least two new nakshikanthas to sell at a craft fair held in the Shilpakala Academy premises in the first week of January. This year she had started the work in October, earlier than usual, because she was also preparing a third quilt as a commission from a woman in Gulshan who had seen her work at the previous year's fair and tracked her down through the organizers three months later. The Gulshan woman had specified she wanted something large enough to cover a queen-sized bed, with a pattern that matched photographs she had emailed to Jharna's neighbor's phone, since Jharna did not have a smartphone. Jharna completed the commission quilt by late November and sent it by courier through the shop near the bus stand. The woman called three days after sending to confirm receipt and said she was very pleased. On the morning of the January fair, Jharna took the bus from Demra at five in the morning and reached Shilpakala by seven to set up her stall. By noon, both quilts she had brought to sell were already gone.

text: Nahid had been asked to deliver a eulogy at the memorial service for his old schoolteacher, Mr. Alam, who had died two weeks ago in Comilla. Mr. Alam had taught Nahid mathematics at a government school in Comilla from 1999 to 2001, and Nahid credited him as the reason he had gone on to study engineering. Nahid had not been back to Comilla in four years. He flew from Dhaka on a Tuesday morning and took a CNG from the airport to the school, which he had not visited since his own graduation ceremony twenty-three years ago. The auditorium had been repainted at some point, but the blackboard in the main hall looked like it might be the original. Before the service, Nahid walked around the school grounds and found the tree behind the science block where he and his friends used to eat lunch. It was significantly taller now. At the service, about a hundred people came, including several of Nahid's former classmates, one of whom he had not spoken to since they both left Comilla for university in the same year. Nahid's eulogy ran seven minutes longer than the five minutes he had been given. Nobody seemed to mind. He returned to Dhaka on the evening flight and was back at his desk by nine the next morning.

text: The fish market in Jashore opened before sunrise every morning and by seven it was already winding down. Yusuf had been buying his stock from the same seller, old Rahim, for six years. On a morning in mid-November, Rahim told him that he was retiring and that his son, who had been working in the Dhaka fish trade for the past four years, would be taking over the stall from the first of next month. Yusuf walked back to his small restaurant on the main road in a distracted mood. He had opened the restaurant eleven years ago in a rented space that his landlord had now threatened to reclaim by February for his own son's use. This was the second time the landlord had mentioned February in the past three months. Yusuf's cook, Jalal, who had been with him since the restaurant's second year, noticed the mood during prep and asked what was wrong. Yusuf told him about Rahim. Jalal said he knew a fish supplier in Magura who delivered to Jashore twice a week and had a reputation for reliable quality, and that he had been meaning to mention the man for some time but kept forgetting. That afternoon Yusuf called the Magura supplier. Three years later, when Yusuf eventually opened a second, larger restaurant two blocks away, the Magura man was still his primary supplier.

text: Selin had grown up hearing about the abandoned textile mill at the edge of her town in Narsingdi, a place her parents had warned her away from as a child. In the first week of her summer break from university in Dhaka, she decided to go with two friends to photograph it. They had done similar urban exploration trips before, once in an old jute mill in Narayanganj six months ago and once in a disused railway building in Tongi that a contact on social media had told them about three months earlier. The Narsingdi mill was harder to access than expected because the fence that had been broken when Selin was a teenager had been partially repaired. They found a gap on the north side and entered in the late morning. Inside, the weaving floor was enormous and dark, with rusted machinery still standing in rows. A night watchman, who turned out to be a sixty-year-old man who lived in a small room attached to the building, found them two hours into their visit. He was not angry. He told them the mill had closed in 1998 following a labor dispute and had been in legal limbo ever since. He had been a worker there from 1991 and had taken the watchman job because he had nowhere else to go. He made them tea on a small stove and showed them an old logbook from 1996 before letting them leave.

text: Kabir had been working the night shift at a security post near a construction site in Dhaka's Bashundhara area for seven months. On a cold January night, around two in the morning, a stray dog appeared at the edge of his post and did not leave. It was injured, limping on one rear leg. Kabir had no particular history of caring for animals, but he gave it a biscuit from his own packet and the dog stayed. Over the following three weeks, the dog slept under the site watchman's lean-to during the day and appeared at Kabir's post each night. The construction site supervisor, a stern man who had worked on projects all over the country from Cox's Bazar to Sylhet, noticed the dog in the third week and said nothing, which Kabir interpreted as permission. In February, when his night shift contract was not renewed and he moved to a new security job at a commercial building in Banani, Kabir asked his cousin who lived in a ground-floor flat in Bashundhara to take in the dog. His cousin agreed reluctantly. Four months later, Kabir visited the flat and found the dog asleep on the sofa next to his cousin, who had by then named it Tara and appeared to have forgotten he was ever reluctant.

text: Tisha had worked as a flight attendant for a domestic airline for six years when the airline suspended operations in October due to financial restructuring. She was based in Dhaka but had been on a layover in Cox's Bazar when the announcement came. She heard about it from a colleague's message while sitting on the beach on a Tuesday afternoon, one day before she was scheduled to fly back. She returned to Dhaka on the only flight that operated the next morning before service was officially halted. Over the following three months, she applied to several positions, including two with international airlines that operated out of Hazrat Shahjalal Airport. In January, while waiting for responses, she took a temporary job as a customer service supervisor at a hotel in Gulshan, a position a former colleague had connected her with. She had worked in hospitality briefly eight years ago, before joining the airline, so it was not entirely unfamiliar. By February she had received interview calls from two of the airlines she had applied to. The first interview, for a Dubai-based carrier, was conducted at a hotel in Karwan Bazar in late February. The second, for a Malaysian airline, was held via video call in the first week of March. She received the Malaysia offer first and accepted it. She started training in Kuala Lumpur in May.

text: Aleem had been driving a rickshaw in Sylhet city for four years. On a rainy afternoon in June, he picked up a passenger outside a private hospital near Amberkhana who asked to go to the Sylhet railway station. The man was elderly, traveling with a large bag, and sat quietly for most of the ride. Near the station, he asked Aleem how long he had been pulling a rickshaw. They talked for a few minutes after the man paid. The man told him he was a retired school headmaster from Moulvibazar who had taught for thirty-eight years and was now traveling to Dhaka to visit his daughter. He had been at the hospital not as a patient but to accompany a former student who was in for surgery. He asked Aleem if he had children. Aleem said he had a daughter in class five and a son who was three. The man took out a visiting card from his shirt pocket and told Aleem to contact him when his daughter was ready for secondary school, because he still knew people in the Moulvibazar education board. He said this without drama, as though it were a simple practical arrangement, and then picked up his bag and walked toward the station entrance. Aleem kept the card in the small tin box where he stored his daily earnings. He did not contact the man for three years, and when he finally did, the man remembered who he was immediately.

text: Lena's first job after finishing a master's degree in environmental science at BUET was with a consultancy firm in Dhaka's Dhanmondi area. The firm had been hired by a district authority in Brahmanbaria to conduct an environmental impact assessment for a proposed industrial zone. She joined the firm in March and was assigned to the Brahmanbaria project three weeks into her employment. Her supervisor, a hydrologist who had spent the previous decade working on river management projects along the Meghna and Brahmaputra, took her on the first field visit in April. They spent four days in Brahmanbaria, meeting local government officials, visiting the proposed site, and walking along the Titas river, which ran adjacent to the zone boundary. On the second day she met a fisherman who had lived by the Titas all his life and described how the river's fish population had declined significantly over the past fifteen years due to upstream pollution from factories established in the 1990s. Back in Dhaka, she submitted her section of the draft report in late May. The final report, incorporating revisions from the district authority, was submitted in August. The following February she learned that the project had been approved with modifications, including a buffer zone along the river that her section of the report had specifically recommended.

text: Khalid had grown up in a seafront town in Cox's Bazar and left for Dhaka at eighteen to study. He was now thirty-four and worked in marketing for a garments export firm in Tejgaon. He visited Cox's Bazar once a year, usually around the time of Eid. This particular year, he arrived a few days after Eid ul Fitr and found his parents' house noisier than usual. His younger sister had given birth seven weeks ago, and the baby was being passed from relative to relative at every hour. His father, now seventy, moved more slowly than Khalid remembered from his visit two years ago. On the second afternoon, Khalid walked the beach alone. The hotel zone had expanded again. Three new structures had gone up in the past year at the northern end that had been empty lots the last time he came. He sat at a tea stall near Laboni beach where an old man was frying fish over a small coal stove, a snack Khalid had been eating at this exact spot since childhood. The tea stall owner recognized him, which surprised him. He had no memory of the man's face. The owner said Khalid's father used to bring him here every year when he was a boy, right up until he left for Dhaka. The owner had been running the stall since 1989. Khalid called his father and asked him to come down to the beach.

text: Feroz had studied fine arts in Dhaka and now lived in Berlin on an artist residency that had started three months ago and was scheduled to run until the end of the year. He had applied for the residency two years earlier, during a particularly difficult financial stretch when he was sharing a studio in Eskaton with two other artists and trying to sell work through a Dhaka gallery that had been struggling with low foot traffic. The acceptance letter had come fifteen months after the application, on a morning when he was in Sylhet visiting his aunt. He had been working in Berlin on a large-scale mixed media series that drew on imagery from the Dhaka waterlogging floods of 2004, which he had lived through as a child in Demra. In October, a Berlin-based art magazine ran a short profile on him and the residency program. His mother, who lived in Demra and had no internet at home, heard about the article from Feroz's cousin in Dhaka who read it on a shared phone screen. Feroz's stipend covered his rent in Berlin's Neukölln district and a modest materials budget. He had eaten at the same Turkish restaurant three nights a week since arriving because it was the only place within walking distance that stayed open past midnight, and he often worked late. He was due to return to Dhaka in December.

text: Riman had always been the quiet type in school. He grew up in Bogura and moved to Dhaka at twenty-two for an IT job that paid less than he had hoped. Three years into that job, while taking night classes in cybersecurity at a training center in Paltan, his employer shut down its Dhaka office and moved operations to Chattogram. Riman did not want to relocate. He spent four months freelancing from a coworking space in Banani while continuing his night classes. He finished the cybersecurity course in August. In September, he received a project inquiry through an online platform from a small financial firm in Singapore that had seen his profile two weeks earlier. The project was a security audit for their internal systems. It took six weeks and paid more than three months of his previous salary. The following January, the same firm offered him a part-time ongoing contract. By March, he had moved from the coworking space to a small office in Gulshan that he shared with two other freelancers he had met at a tech meetup the previous October. He was back in Bogura for Eid that year and told his father, who had spent thirty years working at a government bank, that he now worked for companies he had never met in countries he had never visited. His father thought about that for a while and then said he supposed that was how things were going.

text: Rupa had planted the seeds of the tomatoes in small pots on her apartment balcony in Uttara at the beginning of November. She had read about container gardening in a magazine article three months earlier and had bought supplies from a nursery in Abdullahpur on a Friday afternoon. By late December, the plants had grown tall enough to need stakes. One of her neighbors, an older woman who had been growing plants on her own balcony for fifteen years, came over to look and told Rupa she had overwatered them in the early weeks, which showed in the yellowing of the lower leaves. The woman had grown up in a village in Netrokona where her family had a vegetable garden behind the house that produced enough to share with neighbors every season. She showed Rupa how to trim the lower branches and adjust the drainage. By late January, the first green tomatoes appeared. Rupa photographed them and sent the picture to her mother in Sylhet, who called back and said she had not grown a single vegetable in her entire life but was proud anyway. By mid-February, the tomatoes were ripe. She made a salad and brought a portion to the older neighbor, who tasted it and said it was better than she expected for a first crop and that Rupa should try cucumbers next.

text: Lutfur had been a professional cook at a hotel in Dinajpur for nine years when the hotel was sold to a new owner who brought in his own staff. Lutfur was let go in March with two months of severance. He had savings enough for six months. He spent April visiting his brother in Gaibandha, where he also helped a local restaurant owner with their kitchen setup for two weeks without pay, just to keep his hands busy. In May he returned to Dinajpur and heard from a neighbor that a new resort was opening near the Ramsagar lake, about fifteen kilometers outside town, and was looking for experienced kitchen staff. He went out there one morning on his bicycle and asked to speak with the manager. The manager was not in. He returned four days later. The manager was a young woman from Dhaka who had a hotel management degree and had been given the task of staffing the resort from scratch. She interviewed Lutfur for forty minutes in a half-finished office with no chairs, both of them standing. He was hired as head cook. The resort's soft opening was in July. The first guests arrived from Dhaka, a group of eight who had seen the resort on Instagram two months before it had even opened. Lutfur spent that opening weekend cooking for guests and staff simultaneously, sleeping four hours each night. By September, the resort had its first fully booked weekend.

text: Hana had been corresponding with a pen pal in Japan for two years through a letter-writing program organized by a cultural society she had joined in Dhaka at the recommendation of a colleague. Her pen pal was a woman of about the same age in Osaka, a librarian who had studied Bengali literature at university and could read but not speak the language. They wrote to each other in English. In their second year of correspondence, Hana's pen pal mentioned that she would be visiting Bangladesh for two weeks in December for a heritage travel trip organized through a literary tourism group. Hana volunteered to show her parts of Dhaka that tourists often missed. When her pen pal arrived, Hana took leave from her teaching job at a college in Lalbagh for three days. On the first day they visited the Sadarghat riverfront and the Armenian Church in Armanitola, both of which had been on a list her pen pal had kept for years based on her reading of Bengali novels set in old Dhaka. On the second day, they took a bus to Sonargaon to visit the folk art museum, a trip of about thirty-five kilometers that took longer than expected due to a road diversion set up three days earlier after monsoon damage. In the museum, her pen pal stood for a long time in front of an exhibit on nakshikantha quilting and said she had first read about this form in a short story published in 1950 that she had studied in her second year at university.

text: Mia pushes the empty envelope across the Parisian café table, wondering why Ben is even bothering with the courier run tomorrow when he knows she's flying out to London tonight, though Leo had already blown up her phone yesterday from New York, panicking about the keys he mislaid three days ago in that grimy cab near the UN building, even though Sarah had casually mentioned last week that she'd fished them out of the recycling bin before she cleared out of their Berlin flat two weeks ago—not that Mia cares, especially since she'd spotted them herself under the couch cushions a week ago and decided to let Leo sweat it out for once. Out on the TGV tracks somewhere near Lyon, Ben is currently re-reading Sarah's final text from exactly fourteen days back, the one that ended with a curt period instead of their usual exclamation, and it's making him so restless that he completely forgets the 5 PM board meeting in London he's supposed to chair tonight, the same one Leo is frantically trying to reschedule from his JFK layover right now. Mia rubs her temples, calculating that Leo has about four hours until his touchdown at Heathrow, which gives her just enough time to swing by her Left Bank flat, grab that spare key from her desk drawer—the one she's had since their disastrous coffee meetup in Central Park two months ago—and toss it into an overnight pouch before Ben's delayed train even pulls into St. Pancras, ensuring Leo gets it before sunrise, which would be a satisfying middle finger to the very specific warning she'd given him last Tuesday about trusting Ben with anything valuable during transatlantic handoffs.

text: The quantum decoupler finally arrived at the Nairobi lab this morning, three weeks after Dr. Aris ordered it from the Osaka facility, though the shipping manifest clearly shows it physically left Osaka exactly forty-eight hours ago—a glaring discrepancy that would've made perfect sense if Aris hadn't personally carried a prototype to Geneva last Friday for the demonstration that got cancelled by the funding board, forcing him to repackage it and ship it back to Nairobi over the weekend, where it sat in customs purgatory until this past Tuesday, accumulating a bizarre set of interference readings. Meanwhile, his colleague Priya is currently running cold-start diagnostics on the backup unit in the Mumbai server room, a unit Aris had personally calibrated six months ago during the worst monsoon power-outages, and she's finding error logs timestamped for next Thursday afternoon, which is particularly unsettling because Aris distinctly remembers deleting those exact error logs yesterday evening during his four-hour layover at Dubai International, just before he video-called his supervisor to confirm the Tuesday morning delivery—a call that, according to the metadata on Priya's mobile phone, actually took place three days ago, which is a timestamp she dismisses outright because her phone is still stubbornly set to Tokyo time from the conference she attended there last winter, a conference where she first met Aris over stale sushi and argued about oscillator frequencies, an argument they are still having right now, in real-time, across a patchy satellite link as she stares at the future-dated logs and he stares at the paradoxically early arrival crate sitting in his Nairobi receiving bay.

text: Coach Alvarez paced the Vancouver locker room, yelling at the medical staff to hurry up with Martinez's hamstring wrap because the striker had to board the private jet to Kansas City in under ninety minutes for the second-leg group match, although the starting lineup he'd submitted to FIFA three hours ago still listed Martinez as fit—a deliberate bluff he'd cooked up with the team psychologist over breakfast in Edmonton exactly forty-eight hours prior, right after they'd watched the French squad demolish Portugal in a match that had kicked off at 2 PM local time but which Alvarez had watched on a 5 AM replay due to the god-awful timezone shift from their previous training camp in Morocco six weeks earlier, a camp where Martinez had first tweaked that same hamstring during a midnight sprint drill, an injury he'd kept entirely hidden from the team's lead physician until last Tuesday, when the physician caught him limping toward the team bus outside the Orlando training facility, which forced Alvarez to call an emergency strategy meeting at 11 PM that very night, a meeting that completely overrode the game-plan they'd practiced religiously every morning since the qualifiers in Buenos Aires eight months ago, and now, as the jet engines hummed on the tarmac, Alvarez received a frantic text from his assistant, who was already in Kansas City setting up the equipment, informing him that the French coach had just pulled a similar bluff two hours earlier in the press conference, claiming his star winger was injured when Alvarez knew for a fact—because his data analyst had tracked the winger's commercial flight from Paris to Montreal yesterday afternoon—that the winger was perfectly healthy and currently eating dinner at a steakhouse three blocks from the Kansas City stadium, a steakhouse Alvarez himself had scouted during a layover last spring, back when the World Cup host cities were first announced.

text: Lena clutched her winning ticket, ecstatic that Brazil had just sealed the final spot against the hosts in the 119th minute, though she remembered distinctly that she'd placed the bet at a dodgy sports bar in Seattle last Friday, not the official booth outside the MetLife stadium where she currently stood, because the ticket clearly showed the odds from the group-stage opener between Mexico and Canada—a match she'd missed entirely since she was stuck on a Greyhound from Toronto to Chicago that very afternoon, a ride she'd booked two months in advance to avoid the $800 flight surge, yet here she was, three timezones away from where she started, collecting her winnings exactly one week before the final trophy lift, a timeline that made her head spin because she'd also made a secondary bet with her brother in São Paulo just yesterday, wagering that Brazil would score first in the semi-final against Germany, a semi-final that wouldn't actually happen until next Tuesday, though her brother had insisted on settling the debt immediately using the exchange rate from their last FaceTime call, which had taken place at 2 AM Brasília time while Lena was watching the USA-Netherlands round-of-16 in Philadelphia last Thursday, a match that had gone to penalties and ended so late that she'd missed the last subway train, forcing her to crash on a stranger's couch in Queens, a stranger who turned out to be a FIFA delegate she'd briefly met at the 2022 final in Doha, back when she'd lost a similar bet on Argentina and spent the entire flight home to Bogotá regretting it, which is precisely why she'd diversified her bets this year across three different host cities, starting with the Mexico City opener she'd attended in person three weeks ago, then the Kansas City quarter-final she'd watched from a packed sports bar last Saturday, and now this miraculous final ticket she'd won in a raffle held by the same Greyhound driver who'd driven her from Chicago to Denver exactly five days ago, a driver who had promised her that if Brazil made it to the final, he'd personally fly out to New Jersey to celebrate with her—a promise he'd made at 6 AM Mountain Time, just as the sun rose over the Rockies, which felt like a lifetime ago given the sheer chaos of the past seventy-two hours.

text:
Elias rubbed his tired eyes, reviewing the logs from last week's disaster. The instant the initial software diagnostic wrapped up, the automated system reboot kicked off. Halfway through that restart process, a massive power surge hit the grid. The system eventually finished its reboot, but the electrical anomaly kept wreaking havoc on the building. Deep within the timeframe of that prolonged power surge, the main capacitor violently exploded.

He shifted his focus to the chaotic events of this morning's facility lockdown. According to the timeline, the evacuation siren blared the very second the doors sealed, though it cut out while the building remained secured. Much later in the ordeal, the emergency backup generators roared to life, running steadily until the lockdown was lifted and both shut down in perfect unison.

Now, listening to the overhead servers, Elias noticed a chilling detail on his monitor: the grid's final warning beep synchronized flawlessly from beginning to end with a terrifying radio silence on his team's comms. He could only pray the makeshift wire patch he'd soldered yesterday would hold together well past the safety inspectors' final review arriving tomorrow.

text:
David stared at the malfunctioning fuel injector, recalling last week’s trials. The engine prep phase ended the exact second the primary test-fire began. That test overlapped disastrously with a facility outage; while the primary test-fire was well underway, a grid fluctuation struck, persisting long after the test-fire had finished. Right in the middle of that prolonged power issue, the coolant loop completely failed.

Now, the pressure gauge spiked dangerously into the red. When the facility lockdown triggered this morning, the warning siren initiated at the exact same moment, but faded out while the lockdown was still actively ongoing. Much later, the backup exhaust fans kicked in, humming loudly until both the fans and the lockdown abruptly concluded together.

David realized the engine's final critical redline lasted for the exact same duration as the terrifying telemetry blackout, perfectly mirroring each other. This impending failure would test the containment protocol he coded yesterday—a safety measure installed long before the defense contractors' inspection scheduled for tomorrow.

text: Watching the relentless stream of fatal error logs cascading down the terminal screen in the chilled darkness of the primary datacenter, Lin furiously typed a rollback command, terrified that this data breach was exactly what the anonymous white-hat hacker had warned her about via an encrypted message she decoded on a bullet train to Kyoto last spring. She bypassed the authentication firewall, a security measure the backend team had proudly deployed from the Seattle office the morning after the frantic post-mortem meeting that followed the disastrous beta launch the previous weekend, a launch that had inadvertently exposed user credentials because the cloud storage buckets were misconfigured during a rushed patch pushed from a quiet coffee shop three days prior. If her script didn't execute before the automated defense systems initiated a hard purge on the compromised clusters in the overseas server farm—an event scheduled to happen the moment the network clock struck midnight—the system would irreversibly overwrite the master database backup that she had painstakingly cloned onto a secure drive in her home office yesterday afternoon. The cascading failures on her monitor closely mirrored the algorithmic loop she had accidentally created in a university hackathon a lifetime ago, a mistake that had crashed the campus network just as the judges were evaluating her group's presentation in the main auditorium, leading her to vow she would never again merge untestable code without running the simulation environment she was currently spinning up in the background. Her phone vibrated on the server rack, displaying a frantic incoming call from the lead product manager who was likely pacing in the boardroom awaiting the quarterly earnings report tomorrow morning, completely ignorant of the fact that the financial algorithms they had excitedly signed off on during the week of the summit were currently being manipulated by a rogue process that had been lying dormant in the legacy repository since the original founders sold the company in a cramped garage halfway across the world.

text: Maester Pycelle clutched the raven's scroll, his arthritic fingers trembling as he read the news from Winterfell—news that had been sent three days prior, though the raven had been waylaid by autumn storms over the Neck, meaning Lord Stark had already marched south with his bannermen two fortnights ago, a march Pycelle had explicitly advised against during the small council meeting last Tuesday, the same meeting where Littlefinger had casually mentioned that he'd seen Ser Jaime Lannister departing King's Landing for Casterly Rock exactly a week before that, which made no sense because Pycelle had personally dined with Jaime in the Red Keep's east tower just last night, or rather, the night before last, because the King's nameday feast had run so late that Pycelle had confused the date entirely, a confusion that was only compounded by the raven he'd received from Oldtown this very morning, informing him that the Citadel had confirmed the white raven's message about winter's arrival—a message they'd dispatched six moons ago, which meant the maesters had either been dreadfully slow or the seasons themselves were playing cruel tricks on the realm, though Pycelle suspected the truth was far simpler: Grand Maester Ebrose, who had visited King's Landing exactly one moon turn before Robert's Rebellion began, had always warned him that ravens carrying conflicting timestamps were the first sign of the Long Night's creeping influence, an influence Pycelle had dismissed as maester's folly until Lord Varys appeared in his chambers at the hour of the wolf, three hours past midnight, whispering that he'd received an identical scroll from a Qarthine trader who claimed he'd seen Daenerys Targaryen's dragons flying over the Dothraki Sea, a sighting that had supposedly occurred five weeks ago but the trader's ship had only just docked in Braavos yesterday afternoon, forcing Varys to send a replacement raven to Dragonstone, a raven that would take another four days to arrive, by which time Pycelle knew—with a sinking certainty that curdled his stomach—that the Lannister army, which had marched from the Golden Tooth at dawn this very day, would have already crossed the Trident and engaged the Stark forces in a battle that, according to the celestial calculations he'd completed last fortnight, wasn't supposed to happen until the next full moon.

text: Jotaro Kujo adjusted his cap, staring at the Cairo street where DIO's mansion had stood just yesterday, though the timeline had become hopelessly muddled since Polnareff had activated his Stand's time-acceleration ability during the fight in the alleyway behind the hotel last Tuesday, a fight that had somehow reset the local clock to 11 PM Monday night while the rest of Egypt's timezone stubbornly ticked forward, meaning that Jotaro was simultaneously present at the mansion's destruction—which had occurred three days ago in real-time—and the hotel check-in he'd completed five hours prior, all while receiving a frantic phone call from Joseph Joestar, who was currently in New York City, a full seven timezones behind Cairo, insisting that he'd witnessed the same explosion from his apartment window at 3 AM local time, an explosion that had actually happened in Cairo at noon on Wednesday, which was already a paradox because Jotaro distinctly remembered defeating DIO at sunset on Thursday, a memory that was currently being overwritten by the Stand user's time-loop ability, an ability that DIO had only unlocked during the full moon two months prior when he'd absorbed the blood of the Joestar lineage, a lineage that Kakyoin had described in excruciating detail during their drive from Tokyo to the airport last summer, a drive that had taken exactly four hours and twenty-seven minutes, a duration that Jotaro could still measure precisely because his Stand's chrono-sense was now malfunctioning, presenting him with three distinct timelines: Timeline A, where he'd arrived in Egypt last week and defeated DIO within three days; Timeline B, where the fight had stretched across a full fortnight and concluded with Jotaro's own temporal displacement; and Timeline C, which his grandfather had accidentally created by using Hermit Purple to view a future that was already thirty-six hours behind schedule, a future that showed Jotaro standing exactly where he was now, at 2 PM Cairo time, except the sun was setting and rising simultaneously, and the street vendor selling falafel in the corner had aged exactly twelve years since Jotaro had bought from him this morning, which meant the Stand's ability wasn't just bending time but bending perception itself, forcing Jotaro to fight a battle that had already been won, lost, and drawn, all within the span of a single afternoon that stretched backward to his childhood in Morioh, where he'd first encountered a similar Stand user during the summer of 1999, a summer that was now bleeding into the Cairo winter, scattering events across a temporal map that even DIO's vampiric intellect couldn't navigate without the precise coordinate of the arrowhead—an arrowhead that had been stolen exactly seven days from now, a theft Jotaro was supposed to prevent by traveling to the past, which he'd already done three hours ago, only to realize that the past was now hosting his future self, a self who had already handed him the key to defeating DIO, a key Jotaro was still holding in his pocket, warm from the friction of a timeline that refused to choose a single direction.

text: Giorno Giovanna watched Gold Experience Requiem rewind the bullet's trajectory for the eighteenth time, though he'd stopped counting the loops three iterations ago because the Stand's ability was actively corrupting his memory of the fight's chronology—a fight that had begun in the Colosseum's ruins at dusk last Thursday, escalated to the Tiber riverbank by midnight, and concluded, apparently, in the Roman airport terminal exactly two hours before the match had even started, a fact that made no sense to Mista, who was currently lying on the ground with a gut wound that had healed itself yesterday but would only be inflicted tomorrow, according to the stopwatch Trish had been holding since their departure from Naples three days prior, a stopwatch that now displayed negative time, counting upward into a negative number that corresponded to the exact hour Bucciarati had died—an hour that hadn't happened yet in Giorno's personal timeline but had already occurred twice in the timeline of Diavolo, who was currently skipping across multiple eras simultaneously, erasing entire seconds from the world's memory while simultaneously extending others into agonizing decades, a paradox that had caused Narancia to receive a text message from himself, sent from the future exactly one week ahead, warning him about an assassination attempt that had already failed because Abbacchio had foreseen it using Moody Blues, replaying the events of the assassination's preparation, which had occurred two days prior, over and over again until the original event lost all meaning, leaving Giorno stranded in a temporal fog where the Colosseum was simultaneously under construction during the Roman Empire, hosting the 1960 Olympic Games, and crumbling into ruins under the weight of Diavolo's collapse, all within a five-minute window that stretched from Tuesday to Thursday, depending on which Stand user's perception you trusted, and Giorno trusted none of them, especially not Fugo, who had called from a payphone in Florence exactly six hours ago—or was it six hours from now?—to confirm that the arrow had been moved to a different location, a location that Giorno had already visited yesterday, which was, according to Gold Experience's recalibration, still thirty-one minutes away, meaning that the final confrontation with Diavolo would either occur in the past, be resolved in the present, or manifest as a memory of a future event that Giorno could only access if he stopped breathing entirely and allowed the Stand's infinite loop to synchronize the contradictions into a single, coherent timeline—a timeline that, according to the graffitied wall of the train station he'd passed through last Tuesday, had already been written by a mysterious figure who signed their name with the same birthmark that Giorno had possessed since childhood, a birthmark that appeared on his shoulder exactly two days before he'd joined Passione, a joining that had taken place six months ago but felt, somehow, like it was happening right now, for the very first time.

text: Walter White adjusted his gas mask, staring at the boiling blue liquid that had cooked for exactly the duration of last night's dinner with Skyler, a dinner where she'd passive-aggressively mentioned the second cell phone he'd been hiding in the master bedroom's vent since last Tuesday, a phone that had buzzed with Jesse's frantic voicemail at 3 AM Wednesday morning—or was it Thursday?—warning him that Tuco had resurfaced from the desert after the deal gone wrong, the deal that Walter had orchestrated in the RV's cramped back while Hank was giving his famous "crystal blue" speech at the DEA office the afternoon before, a speech Walter had attended precisely forty-eight hours after his first chemotherapy session at the hospital downtown, the same hospital where he'd run into Jane's father that morning, the morning after the RV had broken down on the outskirts of Albuquerque, a breakdown that had forced Jesse to call his cousin for a tow, a cousin who'd then recognized the distinctive blue tint and offered them a meeting with a distributor in the old industrial park, a meeting that had been scheduled for last Wednesday but got postponed because the distributor's brother had gotten arrested during the cartel raid that had made the evening news the previous Friday, the same raid that had killed two of Gus's men, which meant Gus had called Walter into the chicken farm that Sunday to calmly explain the new safety protocols he'd implemented since the incident at the laundry facility, an incident that had occurred exactly one week before Walter's first-ever cook with Jesse in the desert RV, a cook that had produced a batch so pure that Emilio had tried to steal the recipe during the heated argument that had landed them both in the desert's scorching afternoon sun, an argument that had ended with Walter dissolving Emilio's body in a bathtub while Jesse panicked in the living room, a bathtub that had almost collapsed through the floor of Jesse's aunt's house, a house that Walter had visited again yesterday to retrieve the hidden cash from the floorboards, only to find that Skyler had already been there earlier that same afternoon, confronted by Jesse's girlfriend—the same girlfriend who'd later OD'd in the apartment across from the RV's latest parking spot—and left a note that Walter had crumpled into his pocket before driving to the car wash for his shift, a shift that had started at noon but he'd been two hours late because he'd stopped at the hospital for bloodwork, the results of which were now sitting in an envelope on his desk at the high school, waiting for him to open them during his prep period next Tuesday, a prep period that would occur exactly twenty-four hours after Saul had called to warn him about the wiretap on Hank's phone, a wiretap that had been installed last month during the joint task force's operation against the cartel, an operation that Hank had been leading since the explosion at the nursing home, an explosion that had killed Hector Salamanca just minutes after Walter had visited him the previous Thursday to settle the grudge that had begun when Tuco first kidnapped him and Jesse and drove them to the desert shack where they'd met the twins, the twins who were now supposedly dead but whom Mike had spotted at a diner just yesterday afternoon, a diner located three blocks from the laundromat where Walter's latest batch was currently drying under the watchful eye of a pair of Gus's most trusted men, men who had no idea that Walter had already buried enough cash in the desert to buy a car wash, a house, and a new identity for his entire family, provided he could survive the next forty-eight hours without getting caught in the crossfire of a war that had started the moment he'd first cooked that blue batch in Jesse's basement, a basement that had flooded during the thunderstorm three summers ago, a storm that Walter remembered vividly because it had been the same night he'd first noticed the lump on his lung, the lump that would eventually lead him to this moment, staring at the boiling liquid, wondering if the timing of his life had ever been this perfectly, catastrophically wrong.

text: Bong wiped the sweat from his brow, sorting through the morning's haul at the Payatas dumpsite, the same mountain of refuse where his father had worked every afternoon for three decades until the landslide that had buried half the neighborhood the day before the mayor's election, an election that had been postponed twice due to the typhoon that had flooded the sorting floor last Tuesday, forcing Bong and his crew to relocate to the temporary site near the river, a river that had overflowed during the monsoon season that had arrived three weeks earlier than the forecasters had predicted, a forecast that Bong had ignored because his wife had been in labor at the city hospital that same afternoon, a labor that had lasted through the night and into the following morning, the morning after he'd found the gold necklace in the trash bag from the upscale subdivision, a necklace he'd hidden in his locker until he could pawn it at the shop his cousin ran near the market, a shop that had been robbed the previous Saturday by the gang that had been terrorizing the neighborhood since the police station closed its doors last month due to budget cuts, budget cuts that had been announced the day after the governor had visited the dumpsite to pose for photographs, photographs that had appeared in the newspaper Bong had used to wrap his lunch just yesterday afternoon, a lunch that he'd eaten while listening to the radio broadcast about the landfill expansion that had been approved the previous week, an expansion that would displace the families living on the eastern slope, including his sister's family, who'd been living there since her husband lost his job at the factory two summers ago, a factory that had shut down the day after the earthquake that had damaged the sorting facility, a facility that Bong had helped rebuild during the weekends following the disaster, weekends that had stretched into months because the contractor had disappeared with the government's relief funds, funds that had been allocated during the emergency session that had taken place the afternoon of the landslide, a landslide that Bong had survived because he'd called in sick that morning, a morning he'd spent at the wake of his neighbor's child, a child who'd died from the fever that had swept through the settlement the week after the floods, floods that had contaminated the water supply that the residents had been using since the pipeline burst during the construction of the new highway, a highway that had been inaugurated by the president himself during his visit last year, a visit that had occurred the same week Bong had first noticed the strange chemical smell emanating from the truck that dumped its load every afternoon at precisely the hour when the other workers took their break, a break that Bong had skipped that day because he'd been counting his earnings from the scrap metal he'd sold to the recycling depot the previous Tuesday, a depot that had raised its prices the day after the international commodity report had been released, a report that had predicted the surge in copper demand that Bong had exploited by hoarding the wires he'd collected during the demolition of the old market last spring, a demolition that had forced the vendors to relocate to the temporary stalls near the church, a church where Bong had prayed every Sunday since his mother passed away three winters ago, a winter that had been unusually cold and had killed the mango trees that had shaded the sorting floor, a floor that Bong was standing on now, watching the afternoon sun cast long shadows over the mountains of garbage, realizing that every bag he opened contained fragments of someone else's timeline—a broken clock from last Tuesday, a photograph from a birthday party two years ago, a letter dated the day his father had died—and that his own life was scattered across this dump just as chaotically, buried under layers of temporal debris that only he could sort, if only he could remember which event came first, which happened after the flood, and which had occurred in the brief window between the typhoon's arrival and his daughter's first cry.

text: When I place the black stone on the lectern in the old philosophy hall, I am still arguing with Professor Vale about whether a person remains the same after every memory has been replaced, although the argument began, as I now remember it, during the winter before the hall’s eastern wing burned, when Vale had asked me in the library whether a copied mind would inherit responsibility for an act committed by its original in a laboratory beneath the river. The question mattered because three days before that library conversation, I had promised Mira at the railway station that I would testify against Vale, while Mira herself had already heard the testimony I would give the following spring in a courtroom that had not yet been built. I know this because the recording she sent from the train arrived in my apartment the morning after I met her at the station, though the train had left the city the previous evening and she claimed she was calling from the same platform where, years later, I would find the black stone. During the festival week, Vale demonstrated a memory machine in the university basement, and the machine produced a version of me who insisted that the debate had already ended, while across town my younger self was still writing the first question that would lead to it. The copy disappeared before dawn, but its notebook survived in a café near the harbor, where Mira read it on the afternoon before the eastern wing burned. By the time the fire reached the hall, Vale had already resigned in a letter dated the week after his resignation, and I had decided to defend him because the copy had confessed to the crime that, according to my own memory, I committed. Now, in the present hall, the students are waiting for my answer, the burned wing is visible through the windows though it was rebuilt years ago, and Vale—dead since the summer after the trial—has left me one final question: if I remember becoming someone else, which of us is standing here to answer for what happened yesterday?

she claimed she was calling from the same platform
years later, I would find the black stone

Vale demonstrated a memory machine in the university basement
the machine produced a version of me who insisted that the debate had already ended
across town my younger self was still writing the first question that would lead to it
The copy disappeared before dawn
its notebook survived in a café near the harbor
Mira read it on the afternoon before the eastern wing burned
the fire reached the hall
Vale had already resigned in a letter dated the week after his resignation
I had decided to defend him
the copy had confessed to the crime
according to my own memory, I committed
the students are waiting for my answer
the burned wing is visible through the windows
it was rebuilt years ago
Vale—dead since the summer after the trial—has left me one final question
if I remember becoming someone else
which of us is standing here to answer for what happened yesterday?

text: At the observatory on the mountain, I am preparing to debate whether free will can survive a universe governed by causes, though the telescope is pointed toward a city that vanished before I was born and the notes beside me were written by my future self during a night I remember spending in prison. The debate was first proposed in a crowded café in Buenos Aires, where I told Elias that choice was real because, three days earlier, I had refused to board a bus in Madrid, and that refusal had saved my life; Elias replied that the refusal was inevitable because he had already watched me make it in a recording sent from the bus station the previous afternoon. The recording reached him after he had mailed me a letter from Cairo, although the letter had been written before our café conversation and described an argument we would have in the mountain observatory. During the monsoon season, I found the letter in a locked room beneath a museum in Dhaka, where the curator told me that Elias had visited the room the year before, despite the museum having been closed then because of a flood that occurred after his visit. I took the letter to Madrid, where I missed the bus, while Elias was simultaneously speaking about me in a lecture hall in Oslo, claiming that my decision had been caused by a fear I had not yet experienced. That fear began, according to the prison notes, when I saw the observatory burn during the winter after the debate, although the observatory is standing around me now and the fire has not yet happened. A guard in the notes says I chose to remain silent, but the same page records my speech from the following morning, when I apparently confessed to choosing silence. Now the telescope turns toward the vanished city, Elias’s voice is waiting through the radio, and I must decide whether to enter the debate, knowing that the decision may already be the reason I am standing here.

text: I am standing in a preserved bakery in Pompeii today, where a loaf of bread rests beside a wall that was buried before the baker finished repairing it, although the repair itself began after the earthquake that damaged the bakery and may have continued until the morning the city disappeared. A woman in the neighboring house had arranged a dinner for the evening after the eruption, while her husband had already fled toward the coast during the afternoon when ash began falling over the forum; meanwhile, in Misenum, a naval commander was preparing ships to rescue people from the bay before the first message describing the disaster reached him. The message was carried by a man who had left Pompeii after the streets became impassable, yet a tablet found years later records him buying wine in the city on the day after he supposedly escaped. A child’s graffiti mentions an election that had ended before the wall was painted, while a merchant’s account lists goods delivered after the shop was sealed by ash. Last week, an archaeologist told me the bakery was abandoned yesterday, meaning the previous excavation day, though the ancient baker’s final mark on the wall uses “tomorrow” to refer to a delivery that may have been scheduled for the very morning the volcano erupted. Before the eruption, tremors had already cracked the theater in Pompeii, and after the eruption, survivors in Naples were still searching for relatives whose houses had vanished beneath the ash; at the same time, Pliny was writing from Misenum about events that would not be fully understood until centuries later. I found a coin yesterday beneath a floor that archaeologists had excavated last spring, but the coin was minted after the building was supposedly destroyed, unless the floor was repaired before the eruption and the destruction occurred later than the layer first suggested. Tomorrow I will return to the bakery with the excavation team, because a sealed doorway has just been opened, and behind it lies a letter written by someone who claims to have survived the eruption even though the name on the letter belongs to a person whose body was identified in a house that had already been buried before the letter could have been written.

text: I am tracing a coastline on a navigation chart in Lisbon this afternoon, though the coastline was drawn before the expedition that supposedly discovered it and corrected after the captain who made the correction had already returned to Seville. The captain left Cádiz during the autumn when a royal commission was still debating whether the voyage should sail west, while his navigator had spent the previous summer in Madeira copying a chart that showed an island he would later claim to have found himself. A storm drove the fleet toward the Azores three days before a letter from the court ordered the fleet to avoid the Azores, and by the time that letter reached the harbor, the ships had already been reported missing in the Caribbean. In a monastery near Porto, a monk recorded hearing news of the expedition before the fleet had left Iberia, although his account was written years later by a scribe who had never met him; meanwhile, in Seville, merchants insured cargo against a route that had not yet been officially recognized. The captain’s brother said the map was redrawn after the first landing, but the mapmaker’s apprentice remembered receiving the coordinates before the ship sailed, and a later copy places the landing on an island that had disappeared from charts by the time the captain returned. I found the disputed map last spring in a basement in Lisbon, after a historian in Havana told me that the original had been burned in Madrid during a fire that occurred before the historian’s source was born. Yesterday, I compared the ink with a logbook written aboard the ship, yet the logbook says the captain saw the coastline tomorrow, a phrase that meant “the next day” to the sailor who wrote it but “the future voyage” to the clerk who copied it decades later. The chart will be presented to the museum tomorrow, unless the coordinates prove that the ship reached the coast before departing, which would be impossible except that the captain’s final note—written after his return to Seville and before his death in Lisbon—describes watching his own fleet disappear beyond the horizon from a harbor where the fleet had not yet arrived.

text: I am listening to a dead radio in a museum basement in Warsaw today, although the frequency it receives was transmitted from London decades before the room became a museum and nearly a month after the operator who supposedly sent it had been arrested in Lyon. The message concerns a train leaving Kraków on the morning after a resistance meeting in Paris, but that meeting had been arranged by a courier who was still in Marseille when the invitation reached Paris, and the courier reached Marseille only after hiding a microfilm in a bookshop in Brussels three days before the bookshop was searched by soldiers who had not yet received the order to search it. In the same week, a British analyst in Bletchley Park broke a cipher whose key had been captured in Norway the previous winter, while a Polish mathematician in Madrid was explaining a different method to an officer who would not meet him in London until after the war. My grandmother claimed that her brother heard the radio in Warsaw before the uprising, yet the radio had been dismantled in a safe house near Lublin by the time the uprising began, and the message he remembered was actually recorded by a woman in Budapest who had not yet crossed into Poland. The woman had escaped from a train outside Vienna during the afternoon before a courier was shot in Prague, though the courier’s last letter, written after his death according to the archive, mentions her warning. When I was a child, my grandmother said the warning arrived yesterday, but yesterday in her story meant the night she waited in a cellar while aircraft passed over Warsaw, whereas the same word, spoken by the radio operator in a surviving transcript, referred to the day before he crossed the English Channel. I found the transcript last spring in London, after a historian in Paris showed me a photograph taken before the meeting that the photograph supposedly documented, and the historian had obtained it from a former agent in Rome who had died before the photograph was developed. Tonight, the museum curator insists the radio never worked, yet the speaker has just clicked, and the voice announcing the train’s departure is the voice of my grandmother’s brother, who was officially killed in Prague two weeks before the broadcast was sent.

text: At present, I am copying a faded caravan ledger in a locked archive beneath Samarkand’s old observatory, though the ink I am trying to identify was written in Kashgar long before the observatory’s dome was raised, and the reason I am here at midnight is that the same ledger was found in a merchant’s chest after his caravan disappeared near Merv, three winters after a treaty was signed in Karakorum that had already been broken by the time the treaty’s messenger reached Tabriz. The merchant had left Xi’an during the spring when a Persian astronomer was still measuring shadows in Maragheh, while his brother, who would later accuse him of theft in Baghdad, was crossing the Pamirs with a shipment of silk that had not yet been purchased when their mother died in Dunhuang. A week before the caravan vanished, a Mongol governor in Balkh had ordered a bridge repaired, although the order was written after the bridge collapsed and carried by a rider who had departed before the collapse; meanwhile, in Venice, a mapmaker was copying rumors of Cathay from a traveler who had reached the Black Sea years after the traveler claimed to have seen the Great Khan’s court. The ledger says the merchant reached Samarkand before the festival, but the festival itself occurred after the Persian envoy who supposedly welcomed him had already died in Herat, and three days before that envoy’s death, a letter from Constantinople had warned him not to trust a seal bearing the name of a ruler who had not yet taken the throne. I know this because yesterday, while examining a seal in the archive, I found the merchant’s initials beneath a later repair, though yesterday also refers to the afternoon when I learned in Kashgar that the chest had been opened in Merv, and that discovery came after my guide in Tabriz had already told me the chest was never there. Tomorrow I will carry the ledger to the museum, unless the archivist keeps the promise he made last autumn in Bukhara to destroy it, because the final page—written after the caravan’s disappearance but before the merchant’s reported death—records a journey to Samarkand that I am now certain he made only because he had already read my own name.

text: Shanto refreshed the fest website's analytics dashboard from backstage, watching registration numbers climb for an event that, per the schedule still pinned in the design team's group chat, hadn't opened yet, a discrepancy stemming from the server going live the previous night ahead of the announcement post, itself delayed because the banner artwork wasn't approved until the design lead returned from the printer's shop across the city, a trip made the morning after the domain renewal nearly lapsed — a near-miss traced back to a payment authorization stuck since the week of the sponsor meeting, a meeting that had been moved up after news broke of a rival fest's launch, news that, ironically, wouldn't be public until the following Monday. He thought of the opening ceremony rehearsal happening right now in the auditorium one floor below, where the emcee was reading an introduction referencing the very keynote speaker whose flight, according to the logistics group, hadn't landed yet, though someone swore they'd seen her in the green room an hour ago, perhaps a mix-up with the speaker from last year's fest, held in the wing of the building since converted into a lab. The registration spike on Shanto's screen, he realized, matched almost exactly the numbers from the stress test his team had run three days prior, run using data seeded from the actual event to test load — a test whose results had, through some pipeline error, been written into the live production table, meaning the fest had, in a sense, already happened in the database days before the first guest walked through the gate that, right now, backstage, hadn't even been unlocked.

text: Meherun adjusted the telescope's focus on the rooftop, tracking a comet whose light, she reminded herself, had left its source centuries before the observatory below had even been founded, the same observatory that, decades from now in a future she wouldn't see, was slated for decommissioning — a fact she'd learned last spring from an alumnus who'd once observed this very comet's previous pass, back when the rooftop was still an open field, before the annex was built the year of the club's founding. Her notes referenced a photograph taken the morning after tonight's session, showing cloud cover that hadn't rolled in yet, a photograph she was certain she'd already filed, though the log book on the table beside her remained blank for tonight's date. She thought of Farhan, who was, at this exact moment, calibrating the club's other telescope on a hillside three hours south, having left the city the previous evening after the argument about scope time allocation — an argument that had, strangely, already been resolved in an email sent the following week, one she'd read before it arrived because the club's server synced timestamps incorrectly ever since the migration during last year's eclipse event, an event that itself had been rescheduled from a date now impossible to place, since the original booking conflicted with a meteor shower still three years off. Somewhere below, the club president was locking the gate for the night that had, according to the sign-in sheet, already ended an hour ago, even as Meherun's exposure continued, the shutter still open on a frame that would develop into the very image she'd filed that morning which hadn't happened yet
